title: Finding orthogonal bases
lead: This section builds orthogonal and orthonormal bases out of any basis: Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization takes the basis vectors one at a time and removes from each its orthogonal projection onto the span of those before it, and writing those steps in matrix form leads to the $QR$ factorization of a matrix whose columns are linearly independent.
summary_html:
This section explored the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization algorithm and how it leads to the matrix factorization $\kA=\kQ\kR$ when the columns of $\kA$ are linearly independent.

  • Beginning with a basis $\kvecvone, \kvecvtwo,\ldots,\kvecvn$ for a subspace $\kW$ of ${\mathbb R}^m$, the vectors

    $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecwone & = \kvecvone \\ \kvecwtwo & = \kvecvtwo - \frac{\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecwone}{\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}\kvecwone \\ \kvecwthree & = \kvecvthree - \frac{\kvecvthree\cdot\kvecwone}{\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}\kvecwone - \frac{\kvecvthree\cdot\kvecwtwo}{\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwtwo}\kvecwtwo \\ & \vdots \\ \kvecwn & = \kvecvn - \frac{\kvecvn\cdot\kvecwone}{\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}\kvecwone - \frac{\kvecvn\cdot\kvecwtwo}{\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwtwo}\kvecwtwo - \ldots - \frac{\kvecvn\cdot\kvecwnmone} {\kvecwnmone\cdot\kvecwnmone}\kvecwnmone \end{aligned} $$

    form an orthogonal basis for $\kW$.

  • We may scale each vector $\kvecwi$ appropriately to obtain an orthonormal basis $\kvecuone,\kvecutwo,\ldots,\kvecun$.
  • Expressing the Gram-Schmidt algorithm in matrix form shows that, if the columns of $\kA$ are linearly independent, then we can write $\kA=\kQ\kR$, where the columns of $\kQ$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$ and $\kR$ is upper triangular.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose we have a basis for ${\mathbb R}^2$ consisting of the vectors

$$ \kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 2 \end{array}\right] $$

as shown in Figure 6.4.1. Notice that this basis is not orthogonal.

  1. Find the vector $\kvecvtwohat$ that is the orthogonal projection of $\kvecvtwo$ onto the line defined by $\kvecvone$.
  2. Explain why $\kvecvtwo - \kvecvtwohat$ is orthogonal to $\kvecvone$.
  3. Define the new vectors $\kvecwone=\kvecvone$ and $\kvecwtwo=\kvecvtwo-\kvecvtwohat$ and sketch them in Figure 6.4.2. Explain why $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ define an orthogonal basis for ${\mathbb R}^2$.
  4. Write the vector $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}8 \\ -10 \end{array}\right]$ as a linear combination of $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$.
  5. Scale the vectors $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ to produce an orthonormal basis $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$ for ${\mathbb R}^2$.

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. $\kvecvtwohat = \kvecvone$.
  2. The orthogonal projection $\kvecvtwohat$ is defined so that $\kvecvtwo-\kvecvtwohat$ is orthogonal to $\kvecvone$.
  3. $\kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ are othogonal, which can be checked with the dot product.
  4. The projection formula gives $\kvecb = -\kvecwone -9\kvecwtwo$.
  5. $\kvecuone=\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecutwo=\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kW$ is a three-dimensional subspace of ${\mathbb R}^4$ with basis:

$$ \kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 3 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -3 \\ -3 \\ -3 \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$

We can see that this basis is not orthogonal by noting that $\kvecvone\cdot\kvecvtwo = 8$. Our goal is to create an orthogonal basis $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$ for $\kW$. To begin, we declare that $\kvecwone=\kvecvone$, and we call $\kWone$ the line defined by $\kvecwone$.

  1. Find the vector $\kvecvtwohat$ that is the orthogonal projection of $\kvecvtwo$ onto $\kWone$, the line defined by $\kvecwone$.
  2. Form the vector $\kvecwtwo = \kvecvtwo-\kvecvtwohat$ and verify that it is orthogonal to $\kvecwone$.
  3. Explain why $\kSpan\left\{\kvecwone,\kvecwtwo\right\} = \kSpan\left\{\kvecvone,\kvecvtwo\right\}$ by showing that any linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$ can be written as a linear combination of $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ and vice versa.
  4. The vectors $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ are an orthogonal basis for a two-dimensional subspace $\kWtwo$ of ${\mathbb R}^4$. Find the vector $\kvecvthreehat$ that is the orthogonal projection of $\kvecvthree$ onto $\kWtwo$.
  5. Verify that $\kvecwthree = \kvecvthree-\kvecvthreehat$ is orthogonal to both $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$.
  6. Explain why $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$ form an orthogonal basis for $\kW$.
  7. Now find an orthonormal basis for $\kW$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kvecvtwohat = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.
  2. $\kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$
  3. We have $\kvecvone = \kvecwone$ and $\kvecvtwo = \kvecwtwo + 2\kvecwone$ so a linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvone$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$.
  4. $\kvecvthreehat = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ -4 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. $\kvecwthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$
  6. Since $\kvecvi$ can be written in terms of $\kvecwj$ and vice-versa, these new vectors form a basis for $\kW$.
  7. $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 1/2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/2 \\ 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ -1/2 \end{array}\right] $$

Solution.

  1. $\kvecvtwohat = \frac{\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecwone} {\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}\kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.
  2. $\kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$

  3. We have $\kvecvone = \kvecwone$ and $\kvecvtwo = \kvecwtwo + 2\kvecwone$. Therefore, a linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvone$ can be rewritten as

    $$ c_1\kvecvone+c_2\kvecvtwo = c_1\kvecwone+c_2(\kvecwtwo+2\kvecwone) = (c_1+2c_2)\kvecwone + c_2\kvecwtwo\text{.} $$

    In the same way, $\kvecwone=\kvecvone$ and $\kvecwtwo = \kvecvtwo-2\kvecvone$ so any linear combination of $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvone$.

  4. By the Projection Formula, $\kvecvthreehat = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ -4 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. $\kvecwthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$
  6. We can check that $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$ form an orthogonal set. Since $\kvecvi$ can be written in terms of $\kvecwj$ and vice-versa, these new vectors form a basis for $\kW$.
  7. $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 1/2 \\ 1/2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/2 \\ 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ -1/2 \end{array}\right] $$

exercises.prompt:
Sage can automate these computations for us. Before we begin, however, it will be helpful to understand how we can combine things using a list in Python. For instance, if the vectors v1, v2, and v3 form a basis for a subspace, we can bundle them together using square brackets: [v1, v2, v3]. Furthermore, we could assign this to a variable, such as basis = [v1, v2, v3]. Evaluating the following cell will load in some special commands.

sage.repl.load.load("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidaustinm/ula_modules/master/orthogonality.py", globals())
  • There is a command to apply the projection formula: projection(b, basis) returns the orthogonal projection of b onto the subspace spanned by basis, which is a list of vectors.
  • The command unit(w) returns a unit vector parallel to w.
  • Given a collection of vectors, say, v1 and v2, we can form the matrix whose columns are v1 and v2 using matrix([v1, v2]).T. When given a list of vectors, Sage constructs a matrix whose rows are the given vectors. For this reason, we need to apply the transpose.

Let’s now consider $\kW$, the subspace of ${\mathbb R}^5$ having basis

$$ \kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r}14 \\ -6 \\ 8 \\ 2 \\ -6 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}5 \\ -3 \\ 4 \\ 3 \\ -7 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Apply the Gram-Schmidt algorithm to find an orthogonal basis $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$ for $\kW$.
  2. Find $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-5 \\ 11 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 5 \\ \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kW$.

  3. Explain why we know that $\kvecbhat$ is a linear combination of the original vectors $\kvecvone$, $\kvecvtwo$, and $\kvecvthree$ and then find weights so that

    $$ \kvecbhat = c_1\kvecvone + c_2\kvecvtwo + c_3\kvecvthree. $$
  4. Find an orthonormal basis $\kvecuone$, $\kvecutwo$, for $\kvecuthree$ for $\kW$ and form the matrix $\kQ$ whose columns are these vectors.
  5. Find the product $\kQT\kQ$ and explain the result.
  6. Find the matrix $\kP$ that projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kW$ and verify that $\kP\kvecb$ gives $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection that you found earlier.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $$ \kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}14 \\ -6 \\ 8 \\ 2 \\ -6 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ -4 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ \end{array}\right] $$
  2. $\kvecbhat=\left[\begin{array}{r}-4 \\ 9 \\ -4 \\ -4 \\ 3 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  3. $\kvecbhat=-\frac34\kvecvone+\frac12\kvecvtwo+2\kvecvthree$.
  4. $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}14/\sqrt{336} \\ -6\sqrt{336} \\ 8/\sqrt{336} \\ 2/\sqrt{336} \\ -6/\sqrt{336} \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2/\sqrt{24} \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 2/\sqrt{24} \\ -4/\sqrt{24} \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{12} \\ 3/\sqrt{12} \\ 0 \\ -1/\sqrt{12} \\ -1/\sqrt{12} \\ \end{array}\right] $$
  5. $\kQT\kQ=\kI$
  6. $\kP = \kQ\kQT = \begin{bmatrix} 5/6 & 0 & 1/3 & -1/6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6/7 & -1/7 & -2/7 & -1/7 \\ 1/3 & -1/7 & 4/21 & 1/21 & -1/7 \\ -1/6 & -2/7 & 1/21 & 11/42 & -2/7 \\ 0 & -1/7 & -1/7 & -2/7 & 6/7 \end{bmatrix}$

Solution.

  1. $$ \kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}14 \\ -6 \\ 8 \\ 2 \\ -6 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ -4 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ \end{array}\right] $$
  2. $\kvecbhat=\left[\begin{array}{r}-4 \\ 9 \\ -4 \\ -4 \\ 3 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  3. We know that $\kvecbhat$ is in $\kW$ and $\kvecvone$, $\kvecvtwo$, and $\kvecvthree$ is a basis for $\kW$. We find $\kvecbhat=-\frac34\kvecvone+\frac12\kvecvtwo+2\kvecvthree$.
  4. $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}14/\sqrt{336} \\ -6\sqrt{336} \\ 8/\sqrt{336} \\ 2/\sqrt{336} \\ -6/\sqrt{336} \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2/\sqrt{24} \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 2/\sqrt{24} \\ -4/\sqrt{24} \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{12} \\ 3/\sqrt{12} \\ 0 \\ -1/\sqrt{12} \\ -1/\sqrt{12} \\ \end{array}\right] $$
  5. $\kQT\kQ=\kI$ since the matrix product computes the dot products of the columns of $\kQ$.
  6. $\kP = \kQ\kQT = \begin{bmatrix} 5/6 & 0 & 1/3 & -1/6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6/7 & -1/7 & -2/7 & -1/7 \\ 1/3 & -1/7 & 4/21 & 1/21 & -1/7 \\ -1/6 & -2/7 & 1/21 & 11/42 & -2/7 \\ 0 & -1/7 & -1/7 & -2/7 & 6/7 \end{bmatrix}$

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kA$ is the $4\times3$ matrix whose columns are

$$ \kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 3 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -3 \\ -3 \\ -3 \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$

These vectors form a basis for $\kW$, the subspace of ${\mathbb R}^4$ that we encountered in Activity 6.4.2. Since these vectors are the columns of $\kA$, we have $\kCol(\kA) = \kW$.

  1. When we implemented Gram-Schmidt, we first found an orthogonal basis $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$ using

    $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecwone & = \kvecvone \\ \kvecwtwo & = \kvecvtwo - \frac{\kvecvtwo\cdot\kvecwone}{\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}\kvecwone \\ \kvecwthree & = \kvecvthree - \frac{\kvecvthree\cdot\kvecwone}{\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}\kvecwone - \frac{\kvecvthree\cdot\kvecwtwo}{\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwtwo}\kvecwtwo\text{.} \\ \end{aligned} $$

    Use these expressions to write $\kvecvone$, $\kvecvtwo$, and $\kvecvthree$ as linear combinations of $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$.

  2. We next normalized the orthogonal basis $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$ to obtain an orthonormal basis $\kvecuone$, $\kvecutwo$, and $\kvecuthree$.

    Write the vectors $\kvecwi$ as scalar multiples of $\kvecui$. Then use these expressions to write $\kvecvone$, $\kvecvtwo$, and $\kvecvthree$ as linear combinations of $\kvecuone$, $\kvecutwo$, and $\kvecuthree$.

  3. Suppose that $\kQ = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc} \kvecuone & \kvecutwo & \kvecuthree \end{array} \right]$. Use the result of the previous part to find a vector $\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_1}$ so that $\kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_1} = \kvecvone$.
  4. Then find vectors $\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_2}$ and $\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_3}$ such that $\kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_2} = \kvecvtwo$ and $\kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_3} = \kvecvthree$.
  5. Construct the matrix $\kR = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc} \htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_1} & \htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_2} & \htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_3} \end{array} \right]$. Remembering that $\kA = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc} \kvecvone & \kvecvtwo & \kvecvthree \end{array} \right]$, explain why $\kA = \kQ\kR$.
  6. What is special about the shape of $\kR$?
  7. Suppose that $\kA$ is a $10\times 6$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent. This means that the columns of $\kA$ form a basis for $\kW=\kCol(\kA)$, a 6-dimensional subspace of ${\mathbb R}^{10}$. Suppose that we apply Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to create an orthonormal basis whose vectors form the columns of $\kQ$ and that we write $\kA=\kQ\kR$. What are the shape of $\kQ$ and what the shape of $\kR$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecvone & = \kvecwone \\ \kvecvtwo & = 2\kvecwone + \kvecwtwo \\ \kvecvthree & = -2\kvecwone - 2\kvecwtwo + \kvecwthree \\ \end{aligned} $$
  2. $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecvone & = 2\kvecuone \\ \kvecvtwo & = 4\kvecuone + \sqrt{2}\kvecutwo \\ \kvecvthree & = -4\kvecuone - 2\sqrt{2}\kvecutwo + 2\kvecuthree \\ \end{aligned} $$
  3. $\kvecvone = \kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.
  4. $\kvecvtwo = \kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ \sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvthree=\kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}-4 \\ -2\sqrt{2} \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. We have $\kQ\kR = \begin{bmatrix} \kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_1} & \kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_2} & \kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_3} \end{bmatrix} = \kA$.
  6. $\kR$ is upper triangular.
  7. $\kQ$ will be $10\times6$ and $\kR$ will be $6\times 6$.

Solution.

  1. $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecwone & = \kvecvone \\ \kvecwtwo & = \kvecvtwo - 2\kvecwone \\ \kvecwthree & = \kvecvthree + 2\kvecwone + 2\kvecwtwo \\ \end{aligned} $$

    Therefore,

    $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecvone & = \kvecwone \\ \kvecvtwo & = 2\kvecwone + \kvecwtwo \\ \kvecvthree & = -2\kvecwone - 2\kvecwtwo + \kvecwthree \\ \end{aligned} $$

  2. $\kvecwi = \left|\kvecwi\right|\kvecui$ so we have

    $$ \kvecwone = 2\kvecuone,\hspace{24pt} \kvecwone = \sqrt{2}\kvecutwo,\hspace{24pt} \kvecwone = 2\kvecuthree\text{.} $$

    This leads to

    $$ \begin{aligned} \kvecvone & = 2\kvecuone \\ \kvecvtwo & = 4\kvecuone + \sqrt{2}\kvecutwo \\ \kvecvthree & = -4\kvecuone - 2\sqrt{2}\kvecutwo + 2\kvecuthree \\ \end{aligned} $$
  3. Since $\kvecvone = 2\kvecuone$, we have $\kvecvone = \kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.
  4. In the same way, we have $\kvecvtwo = \kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ \sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvthree=\kQ\left[\begin{array}{r}-4 \\ -2\sqrt{2} \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. We have $\kQ\kR = \begin{bmatrix} \kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_1} & \kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_2} & \kQ\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_3} \end{bmatrix} = \kA$.
  6. $\kR=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & -4 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} & -2\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ \end{bmatrix}$ so $\kR$ is upper triangular.
  7. $\kQ$ will be $10\times6$ and $\kR$ will be a $6\times 6$ upper triangular matrix.

exercises.prompt:
As before, we would like to use Sage to automate the process of finding and using the $QR$ factorization of a matrix $\kA$. Evaluating the following cell provides a command QR(A) that returns the factorization, which may be stored using, for example, Q, R = QR(A).

sage.repl.load.load("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidaustinm/ula_modules/master/orthogonality.py", globals())

Suppose that $\kA$ is the following matrix whose columns are linearly independent.

$$ \kA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 5 \\ \end{bmatrix}. $$
  1. If $\kA=\kQ\kR$, what is the shape of $\kQ$ and $\kR$? What is special about the form of $\kR$?
  2. Find the $QR$ factorization using Q, R = QR(A) and verify that $\kR$ has the predicted shape and that $\kA=\kQ\kR$.
  3. Find the matrix $\kP$ that orthogonally projects vectors onto $\kCol(\kA)$.
  4. Find $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ -17 \\ -14 \\ 22 \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kCol(\kA)$.
  5. Explain why the equation $\kA\kvecx=\kvecbhat$ must be consistent and then find $\kvecx$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kQ$ is $4\times3$ and $\kR$ is a $3\times3$ upper triangular matrix.

  2. We see that

    $$ \kQ=\begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{10} & -3/\sqrt{23} \\ 0 & 2/\sqrt{10} & -3/\sqrt{23} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{10} & 1/\sqrt{23} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} & 2/\sqrt{10} & 2/\sqrt{23} \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kR = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{10} & \sqrt{10} \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{23} \end{bmatrix} $$
  3. $\kP=\kQ\kQT = \begin{bmatrix} 569/690 & 22/115 & 209/690 & -44/345 \\ 22/115 & 91/115 & -38/115 & 16/115 \\ 209/690 & -38/115 & 329/690 & 76/345 \\ -44/345 & 16/115 & 76/345 & 313/345 \\ \end{bmatrix}$
  4. $\kvecbhat = \left[\begin{array}{r}-7 \\ -5 \\ 5 \\ 14 \end{array}\right]$
  5. $\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]$.

Solution.

  1. $\kQ$ is $4\times3$ and $\kR$ is a $3\times3$ upper triangular matrix.

  2. We see that

    $$ \kQ=\begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{10} & -3/\sqrt{23} \\ 0 & 2/\sqrt{10} & -3/\sqrt{23} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{10} & 1/\sqrt{23} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} & 2/\sqrt{10} & 2/\sqrt{23} \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kR = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{10} & \sqrt{10} \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{23} \end{bmatrix} $$
  3. $\kP=\kQ\kQT = \begin{bmatrix} 569/690 & 22/115 & 209/690 & -44/345 \\ 22/115 & 91/115 & -38/115 & 16/115 \\ 209/690 & -38/115 & 329/690 & 76/345 \\ -44/345 & 16/115 & 76/345 & 313/345 \\ \end{bmatrix}$
  4. $\kvecbhat = \kQ\kQT\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-7 \\ -5 \\ 5 \\ 14 \end{array}\right]$
  5. Since $\kvecbhat$ is in $\kCol(\kA)$, the system $\kA\kvecx=\kvecbhat$ must be consistent. We find a solution by augmenting $\kA$ by $\kvecbhat$ and row reducing: $\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that a subspace $\kW$ of ${\mathbb R}^3$ has a basis formed by

$$ \kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Find an orthogonal basis for $\kW$.
  2. Find an orthonormal basis for $\kW$.
  3. Find the matrix $\kP$ that projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kW$.
  4. Find the orthogonal projection of $\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kW$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

$\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{5} \\ -1/3 & 2/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\kR = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 6 \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix}$

Solution.

Applying Gram-Schmidt, we have $\kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ -2 \\ 4 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 6 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, which leads to $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2/3 \\ -1/3 \\ 2/3 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$. It therefore follows that $\kvecvone = 6\kvecuone$ and $\kvecvtwo = 6\kvecuone + 3\sqrt{5}\kvecutwo$. This leads to $\kA=\kQ\kR$ where $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{5} \\ -1/3 & 2/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\kR = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 6 \\ 0 & 3\sqrt{5} \end{bmatrix}$.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the basis of ${\mathbb R}^3$ given by the vectors

$$ \kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ -5 \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$
  1. Apply the Gram-Schmit orthogonalization algorithm to find an orthonormal basis $\kvecuone$, $\kvecutwo$, $\kvecuthree$ for ${\mathbb R}^3$.
  2. If $\kA$ is the $3\times3$ whose columns are $\kvecvone$, $\kvecvtwo$, and $\kvecvthree$, find the $QR$ factorization of $\kA$.

  3. Suppose that we want to solve the equation $\kA\kvecx=\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-9 \\ 1 \\ 7 \end{array}\right]$, which we can rewrite as $\kQ\kR\kvecx = \kvecb$.

    1. If we set $\kvecy=\kR\kvecx$, the equation $\kQ\kR\kvecx=\kvecb$ becomes $\kQ\kvecy=\kvecb$. Explain how to solve the equation $\kQ\kvecy=\kvecb$ in a computationally efficient manner.
    2. Explain how to solve the equation $\kR\kvecx=\kvecy$ in a computationally efficient manner.
    3. Find the solution $\kvecx$ by first solving $\kQ\kvecy = \kvecb$ and then $\kR\kvecx = \kvecy$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ -1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right], $$
  2. $$ \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{6} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} & 0 & -2/\sqrt{6} \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kR = \begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} & -\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 2\sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix} $$
    1. $\kvecy = \kQT\kvecb$.
    2. $\kR$ is upper triangular
    3. $\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$

Solution.

  1. We find that

    $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ -1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right], $$
  2. $$ \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{6} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} & 0 & -2/\sqrt{6} \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kR = \begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} & -\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 2\sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix} $$
    1. Since $\kQT\kQ = \kI$, we have $\kvecy = \kQT\kvecb$.
    2. $\kR$ is upper triangular so this equation can be solved using back substitution.
    3. $\kvecx = \left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$

exercises.prompt:
Consider the vectors

$$ \kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \\ 4 \\ -4 \\ 2 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}5 \\ -4 \\ -3 \\ 7 \\ 1 \\ \end{array}\right] $$

and the subspace $\kW$ of ${\mathbb R}^5$ that they span.

  1. Find an orthonormal basis for $\kW$.
  2. Find the $5\times5$ matrix that projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kW$.
  3. Find $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}-8 \\ 3 \\ -12 \\ 8 \\ -4 \\ \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kW$.
  4. Express $\kvecbhat$ as a linear combination of $\kvecvone$, $\kvecvtwo$, and $\kvecvthree$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $$ \kvecwone =\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo =\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwthree =\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} $$
  2. $$ \begin{bmatrix} 7/10 & -1/5 & 3/10 & 1/5 & 1/5 \\ -1/5 & 1/5 & 1/5 & -1/5& -1/5 \\ 3/10 & 1/5 & 7/10 & -1/5 & -1/5 \\ 1/5 & -1/5 & -1/5 & 7/10 & -3/10 \\ 1/5 & -1/5 & -1/5 & -3/10 & 7/10 \\ \end{bmatrix} $$
  3. $\kvecbhat = \left[\begin{array}{r}-9 \\ -1 \\ -11 \\ 7 \\ -5 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  4. $\kvecbhat = \kvecvone - \frac83\kvecvtwo -\kvecvthree$

Solution.

  1. Applying Gram-Schmidt gives us

    $$ \kvecwone =\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo =\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwthree =\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} $$

  2. Let $\kQ$ be the matrix whose columns are the orthonormal basis that results from Gram-Schmidt. Then

    $$ \kQ\kQT = \begin{bmatrix} 7/10 & -1/5 & 3/10 & 1/5 & 1/5 \\ -1/5 & 1/5 & 1/5 & -1/5& -1/5 \\ 3/10 & 1/5 & 7/10 & -1/5 & -1/5 \\ 1/5 & -1/5 & -1/5 & 7/10 & -3/10 \\ 1/5 & -1/5 & -1/5 & -3/10 & 7/10 \\ \end{bmatrix} $$
  3. $\kvecbhat = \kQ\kQT\kvecb = \left[\begin{array}{r}-9 \\ -1 \\ -11 \\ 7 \\ -5 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  4. $\kvecbhat = \kvecvone - \frac83\kvecvtwo -\kvecvthree$

exercises.prompt:
Consider the set of vectors

$$ \kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. What happens when we apply the Gram-Schmit orthogonalization algorithm?
  2. Why does the algorithm fail to produce an orthogonal basis for ${\mathbb R}^3$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. We find $\kvecw=\kveczero$.
  2. This set of vectors is linearly dependent.

Solution.

  1. We find

    $$ \kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right] $$

    Since $\kvecwthree=\kveczero$, this does not produce a basis for ${\mathbb R}^3$.

  2. The vector $\kvecvthree=2\kvecvone-\kvecvtwo$ so this set of vectors is linearly dependent. Since $\kvecvthree$ is in the span of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$, projecting $\kvecvthree$ into that subspace gives $\kvecvthreehat = \kvecvthree$ so that $\kvecwthree = \kvecvthree - \kvecvthreehat = \kveczero$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kA$ is a matrix with linearly independent columns and having the factorization $\kA=\kQ\kR$. Determine whether the following statements are true or false and explain your thinking.

  1. It follows that $\kR=\kQT\kA$.
  2. The matrix $\kR$ is invertible.
  3. The product $\kQT\kQ$ projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kCol(\kA)$.
  4. The columns of $\kQ$ are an orthogonal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.
  5. The orthogonal complement $\kCol(\kA)^\perp = \kNul(\kQT)$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. True
  2. True
  3. False
  4. True
  5. True

Solution.

  1. True. Since $\kQT\kQ=\kI$, we have $\kQT\kA = \kQT\kQ\kR = \kR$.
  2. True. Since $\kR$ is upper triangular and the diagonal entries of $\kR$ are the lengths of the nonzero vectors $\kvecwj$, we have $\det(\kR)\neq 0$, which means that $\kR$ is invertible.
  3. False, because $\kQT\kQ=\kI$.
  4. True. In fact, they are an orthonormal basis for $\kCol(\kA)$.
  5. True. If $\kQT\kvecx = \kveczero$, then $\kvecui\cdot\kvecx=0$ for every vector in an orthonormal basis of $\kCol(\kA)$. Therefore, $\kvecx$ is orthogonal to $\kCol(\kA)$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose we have the $QR$ factorization $\kA=\kQ\kR$, where $\kA$ is a $7\times 4$ matrix.

  1. What is the shape of the product $\kQ\kQT$? Explain the significance of this product.
  2. What is the shape of the product $\kQT\kQ$? Explain the significance of this product.
  3. What is the shape of the matrix $\kR$?
  4. If $\kR$ is a diagonal matrix, what can you say about the columns of $\kA$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $7\times7$
  2. $4\times4$
  3. $4\times4$
  4. They form an orthogonal set.

Solution.

  1. $\kQ\kQT$ is $7\times7$ and projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kCol(\kA)$.
  2. $\kQT\kQ$ is the $4\times4$ identity matrix because the product computes dot products between the columns of $\kQ$.
  3. $\kR$ is a $4\times4$ upper triangular matrix.
  4. The columns of $\kA$ form an orthogonal set.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose we have the $QR$ factorization $\kA=\kQ\kR$ where the columns of $\kA$ are $\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf a}_1},\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf a}_2},\ldots,\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf a}_n}$ and the columns of $\kR$ are $\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_1},\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_2},\ldots,\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_n}$.

  1. How can the matrix product $\kAT\kA$ be expressed in terms of dot products?
  2. How can the matrix product $\kR^T\kR$ be expressed in terms of dot products?
  3. Explain why $\kAT\kA=\kR^T\kR$.
  4. Explain why the dot products $\kvecai\cdot\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf a}_j} = \kvecri\cdot\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_j}$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kvecai\cdot\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf a}_j}$
  2. $\kvecri\cdot\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_j}$
  3. $\kAT\kA = (\kQ\kR)^T(\kQ\kR) = \kR^T\kR$
  4. This follows from the previous parts of this exercise.

Solution.

  1. The entries of $\kAT\kA$ are the dot products $\kvecai\cdot\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf a}_j}$.
  2. The entries of $\kR^T\kR$ are the dot products $\kvecri\cdot\htmlClass{kv-vector}{{\mathbf r}_j}$.
  3. $\kAT\kA = (\kQ\kR)^T(\kQ\kR) = \kR^T\kQT\kQ\kR = \kR^T\kI\kR = \kR^T\kR$
  4. This follows from the previous parts of this exercise.

footnotes.html: The book prints “a linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvone$”; the combination meant is of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$.
The book prints “a linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvone$”; the combination meant is of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$.
The book prints “a linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvone$” again; the combination meant is of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$.
The second entry of $\kvecuone$ prints as $-6\sqrt{336}$; it is $-6/\sqrt{336}$, since $\kvecuone = \kvecwone/\left|\kvecwone\right|$ and $\left|\kvecwone\right| = \sqrt{336}$.
The second entry of $\kvecuone$ prints as $-6\sqrt{336}$ here too; it is $-6/\sqrt{336}$.

The book writes $\kvecwone$ on the left of all three equations; they are $\kvecwone = 2\kvecuone$, $\kvecwtwo = \sqrt{2}\kvecutwo$ and $\kvecwthree = 2\kvecuthree$, since $\left|\kvecwone\right| = 2$, $\left|\kvecwtwo\right| = \sqrt{2}$ and $\left|\kvecwthree\right| = 2$.

These weights do not give $\kvecbhat$: $\kvecvone - \frac83\kvecvtwo - \kvecvthree$ has first entry $-28/3$. Solving $c_1\kvecvone + c_2\kvecvtwo + c_3\kvecvthree = \kvecbhat$ gives $\kvecbhat = 2\kvecvone - 3\kvecvtwo - \kvecvthree$, which is the $\kvecbhat$ of part c.
As in the answer, the weights are $2$, $-3$ and $-1$: $\kvecbhat = 2\kvecvone - 3\kvecvtwo - \kvecvthree$.
The book prints $\kvecw$; the vector that comes out zero is $\kvecwthree$, as the solution says.
